newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ministers set 1998 date on EMU launch members.
newsitem.headline: Ministers set 1998 date on EMU launch members.

text.p: EU finance ministers on Saturday brought Europe's planned single currency one step closer by agreeing to decide on initial membership around the start of May next year.
While not wanting to specify a date, the 15 ministers strongly hinted the decision might be taken over the first weekend of May, which includes a public holiday in many European countries.
Asked by reporters whether the membership decision would be taken over the May Day holiday, Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said, "For some people."

The planned common currency, called the euro, is due to be introduced among banks, governments and financial markets on January 1, 1999, with notes and coins expected in public hands no later than 2002.

Saturday's informal ministerial gathering also reached agreement on a so-called stability pact designed to penalise governments running excessive fiscal deficits under economic and monetary union (EMU), and a revamped exchange rate mechanism that would link the common currency with those not participating in 1999.
"Everything is ready for the changeover to the single currency," French finance minister Jean Arthuis told a news conference.

Efforts to establish the single currency, called the euro, have been hampered in recent weeks by speculation that a number of governments, in particular Germany, would need more time to put their public finances in order.
But Saturday's gathering in the Dutch coastal town appeared to give fresh momentum to the bloc's single currency drive.

European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy told reporters that recommendations from the European Commission and the European Monetary Institute on which states should be in the first wave of EMU would be ready by the end of March, 1998.

There would then be a period of four to five weeks for consultation with national parliaments, before finance ministers and heads of state met over a weekend to finalise the choice of who would join the euro in January 1999.
The ministers, cheered by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to stand for re-election next year, earlier dotted the 'i's and crossed the 't's on the text of the stability pact.
Specifically, they agreed that governments running deficits above three percent of Gross Domestic Product would face a maximum penalty of 0.5 percent of total economic output per year.

During the first year the fine would include a fixed portion, 0.2 percent of GDP, and a variable portion -- an additional 0.1 percent of GDP for every percentage point the deficit exceeds the three percent threshold.
Should the offending government fail to bring its finances under control, additional fines, essentially the variable component, would be levied for every year above the target.

While the maximum annual penalty of 0.5 percent of GDP was agreed by EU leaders last December in Dublin, Saturday's deal could in practice mean a much heavier penalty if the deficit lasted for several years.
"In Dublin we had designed the plans for the building, today we have laid down the foundations," France's Arthuis told reporters.
